title: Value Proposition
in30Seconds: A value proposition is a concise, customer-centered claim about the benefit an offering is expected to provide in a particular situation. It connects a defined customer or user, the job or need at hand, the relevant benefit, and—when warranted—a meaningful difference from alternatives. It is not a feature list, a slogan, a guaranteed result, or proof that people will choose the offering. Early value propositions contain assumptions that evidence may revise.
whyItMatters: A team can describe its product perfectly and still leave the central question unanswered: why would this particular customer find it useful now? A precise value proposition helps students connect an offering to a customer’s context, distinguish benefits from product features, and make a limited comparison with alternatives. It also exposes assumptions before they become confident-sounding claims. That clarity supports later work on customer discovery, product-market fit, business models, and marketing without pretending that a well-written statement alone creates demand or guarantees a viable venture.
learningObjectives: Define a value proposition as a customer-centered claim about an expected benefit in a specified context.
Identify the customer, job or need, benefit, and alternative in a value-proposition statement.
Distinguish a feature from the customer benefit that feature may help create.
Explain how differentiation depends on a relevant comparison rather than novelty alone.
Revise an overbroad value proposition to make its assumptions and limits clearer.

collegeVersion.heading: A value proposition explains expected customer value
collegeVersion.body:
A value proposition is a claim about why an offering may be worth choosing for a particular customer in a particular context. OpenStax describes it as a summary of the benefits a customer can expect from a product or service. The emphasis is on the customer’s expected value, not simply on the venture’s effort or the technical description of the offering. A useful statement therefore answers four connected questions: Who is the customer or user? What are they trying to accomplish, avoid, or improve in this situation? What benefit does the offering claim to provide? Compared with what current option or alternative?

Consider the difference between “We built a scheduling dashboard” and “For independent tutors coordinating recurring sessions, a shared change record can reduce time spent reconciling conflicting messages.” The first names an artifact. The second names a group, a context, and an expected practical benefit. It still does not prove that the dashboard produces that benefit for all tutors, that the benefit is large enough to matter, or that the offering will be chosen. Those are separate questions. A value proposition is a disciplined claim to examine, not a conclusion earned by writing it down.

The word value is deliberately broader than a low price. Depending on the customer and situation, value can mean completing a task with less time, fewer errors, less effort, greater access, clearer information, more reliability, or a better fit with an important preference. One offering may create different kinds of value for different groups. A newspaper, for example, might help readers stay informed while helping advertisers reach an audience. Collapsing those groups into one generic “customer” usually makes the statement vague. The proposition should specify whose perspective is being described.

collegeVersion.heading: Customer, job, and context make the claim testable
collegeVersion.body:
A customer label alone is usually too broad. “Students,” “small businesses,” and “busy parents” contain people with different goals, constraints, and alternatives. A value proposition becomes more precise when it locates a job or need in context. In jobs-to-be-done language, a job is what a person is trying to accomplish in a given circumstance; it can have functional, social, or emotional dimensions. This lesson uses that idea as a framing aid, not as a law of customer behavior. It helps a writer move from a demographic label toward a situation that could make an offering relevant.

For example, a campus equipment-lending service might state: “For students who need a laptop during an unexpected repair, the service aims to provide a working device quickly enough to keep coursework moving.” The relevant job is continuing coursework during a disruption. “Students” is narrowed by the repair context. “Quickly enough” expresses a benefit but also points to an assumption: the turnaround matters to this group. A different proposition could be needed for students who want a device for a full semester, because their constraints and alternatives differ.

Specificity should not turn into a fictional certainty. Phrases such as “will save every customer hours” or “the only solution people need” go beyond what a draft value proposition can establish. Better language marks the scope of the claim: “is designed to,” “aims to,” or “can help” are appropriate when the benefit remains an assumption. Existing data may describe a population or market condition, but, as the SBA notes, broad existing sources may not be specific to one audience. Evidence about a particular group’s context belongs in the related customer-discovery and research work. Here, the writing task is to state the assumption clearly enough that later evidence could support, qualify, or contradict it.

collegeVersion.heading: Features are means; benefits are outcomes for the customer
collegeVersion.body:
A feature is a characteristic of the offering: a shared calendar, offline access, a two-hour delivery window, or a reminder setting. A benefit is the positive result the customer may obtain because of that characteristic: fewer missed changes, the ability to work without a connection, less waiting, or greater confidence that an appointment will be remembered. The same feature can matter differently across contexts. Offline access may be central for a field worker with limited connectivity and nearly irrelevant for a customer who is always online. That is why feature lists cannot substitute for a value proposition.

The distinction also protects against unsupported leaps. A team may accurately say that its product includes automated reminders. It may hypothesize that reminders reduce missed appointments for a defined group. It may not claim that the feature makes its service universally superior, improves every customer’s life, or guarantees a financial outcome without relevant evidence. OpenStax similarly frames customer value in terms of benefits such as doing something more easily, quickly, or at lower cost, rather than merely enumerating product attributes.

A short drafting check is useful: after each feature, ask “so that the customer can…?” If the answer names a plausible outcome in a real situation, the writer is approaching a benefit. If the answer only repeats a technical capability, the statement still describes the product from the inside. This is not a request to invent a marketing slogan. It is a reasoning step that links a proposed means to a claimed customer outcome and reveals where that link is still an assumption.

collegeVersion.heading: Differentiation is a relevant contrast, not a boast
collegeVersion.body:
Differentiation explains why the expected benefit may be meaningfully distinct from the alternatives a customer already has. Alternatives include direct competitors, familiar workarounds, doing nothing, and combining existing tools. “New” or “innovative” is not differentiation by itself; an unfamiliar feature has little value if it does not improve a job the customer cares about. OpenStax’s competitive-analysis discussion distinguishes a product’s unique selling proposition from a venture-level competitive advantage and emphasizes examining customer needs alongside competitor offerings. The useful lesson here is narrow: a value proposition should make a customer-relevant contrast rather than announce that an offering is best.

Return to the tutor example. “Our dashboard has color-coded messages” is a feature. “Unlike separate message threads, a shared change record gives the tutor one place to check the latest schedule update” is a differentiating claim tied to a specific alternative and benefit. It remains conditional. It could fail if tutors already use a reliable shared system, if color coding is confusing, or if the workflow creates new effort. A careful writer avoids treating a difference as proof of superiority.

A compact value-proposition draft can therefore use this pattern: “For [defined customer] who need to [job or need] when [context], [offering] is designed to [specific benefit], unlike [relevant alternative], because it [relevant mechanism or difference].” This is a writing scaffold, not a business-model canvas, a pricing rule, or a validation method. Its purpose is to surface the assumptions: that this customer has the job, that the benefit matters, that the alternative is real, and that the stated difference can plausibly produce the benefit. Those assumptions should remain visible until evidence warrants greater confidence.

vocabulary.definition: A customer-centered claim about the benefit an offering is expected to provide in a defined situation.
A group of potential customers with a relevant shared characteristic, need, or context for an offering.
A task, goal, or progress a person is trying to accomplish in a particular circumstance.
A characteristic or capability of an offering, such as a tool, component, setting, or service attribute.
A positive outcome a customer may obtain from using an offering in a relevant situation.
A customer-relevant difference between an offering and a meaningful alternative that may affect the expected benefit.
A proposition treated as provisionally true for planning or analysis before adequate evidence establishes it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine you are choosing a backpack for a rainy walk to school. A label that says “waterproof zipper, three pockets, blue fabric” tells you its features. A statement that says “helps students keep books dry and easy to find during a wet commute” explains the value it hopes to give a certain person in a certain situation. The second statement still needs checking. Maybe students care more about comfort, maybe another bag already works, or maybe the zipper leaks.

A value proposition is that second kind of statement. It says who an offering is for, what that person is trying to do, and how the offering may help. It should not pretend that every person wants it or that the benefit is already proven.
eli10.analogy: A value proposition is like a note on a tool shelf: “Use this wrench when a bolt is hard to reach; its angled handle gives you room to turn it.” The note identifies the user’s situation, the helpful result, and what is different about the tool. It does more than list that the wrench is metal and six inches long.
eli10.analogyLimits: People are not bolts, and customer choices involve preferences, habits, costs, trust, and alternatives that a tool shelf cannot show. A value proposition can describe a hoped-for fit, but it cannot by itself prove that customers will choose an offering or that a venture will succeed.

workedExample: A campus team proposes a service that loans laptops for short periods when a student’s device is unexpectedly being repaired. Its first sentence is, “We have a fast laptop checkout system with QR codes and text reminders.” That identifies features, but not the value. The team revises it: “For students whose primary laptop is suddenly unavailable during the term, the service is designed to provide a working replacement quickly enough to keep coursework moving, unlike an informal search for a spare device, because verified campus inventory can be reserved in one place.” The claim identifies a customer, context, job, benefit, alternative, and mechanism. It also contains assumptions: that repairs create an urgent interruption, that a quick loan matters, that informal borrowing is a real alternative, and that campus inventory can meet the timing claim. QR codes may support the mechanism, but they are not themselves the customer benefit. The statement is useful because it makes those assumptions visible; it does not validate the service, set a price, or predict adoption.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a feature list as though it were a value proposition.
commonMistakes.correction: State the customer outcome the feature is intended to help create in a specified context.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling everyone the customer.
commonMistakes.correction: Name a defined group and the situation in which the claimed benefit matters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating novelty as proof of differentiation.
commonMistakes.correction: Compare the offering with a relevant existing alternative and describe a customer-relevant difference.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stating an expected benefit as a guaranteed outcome.
commonMistakes.correction: Mark early claims as assumptions and avoid promises that the available evidence cannot support.

compareContrast.distinction: A feature is a capability of the offering; a benefit is the customer outcome that capability may help produce in context.
A value proposition specifies customer, context, and expected benefit; a slogan may be memorable without making those elements clear.
Differentiation is a relevant contrast with alternatives; novelty only indicates that something is unfamiliar or new.

keyTakeaway: A value proposition is a bounded claim about customer value, not a list of features or a promise of success. It earns clarity by naming the customer, context, expected benefit, relevant alternative, and assumptions that still require evidence.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best defines a value proposition?
options: A customer-centered claim about an expected benefit from an offering in a defined context.
A complete plan for funding, operating, and pricing a venture.
A list of every technical characteristic of a product.
A guarantee that customers will purchase an offering.
questionBank.explanation: A value proposition describes expected customer value in context. A is correct; B is a broader business-planning task, C lists features rather than benefits, and D turns a claim into an unsupported guarantee.
questionBank.skill: Recall the customer-centered definition of a value proposition.

questionBank.prompt: A tutoring platform lists “automated reminders” as a feature. Which option states the related benefit most clearly?
options: The platform contains a reminder setting in its menu.
Tutors may spend less time manually following up on upcoming sessions.
Automated reminders are newer than every competing tool.
Every tutor will avoid all missed sessions.
questionBank.explanation: B describes a possible outcome for a customer. A repeats the feature, C makes an unsupported novelty claim, and D promises a universal result that the feature alone cannot establish.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish a product feature from an expected customer benefit.

questionBank.prompt: Which draft is most specific about the customer and context?
options: Our tool makes organizing easier for everyone.
The best new productivity tool on the market.
For volunteer coordinators scheduling last-minute shift changes, the tool is designed to show the current assignment in one shared place.
A modern dashboard with colorful icons and fast servers.
questionBank.explanation: C names a defined group, a situation, and an expected benefit. A is overbroad, B is an unsupported boast, and D describes attributes without explaining customer value.
questionBank.skill: Identify customer and context in a value-proposition draft.

questionBank.prompt: Why is “unlike separate message threads, one shared change record gives tutors one current schedule to check” a differentiation claim rather than merely a novelty claim?
options: It proves the offering has no competitors.
It sets a final price for the service.
It explains the venture’s entire business model.
It compares a customer-relevant benefit with a specific alternative.
questionBank.explanation: D is correct because the statement identifies an alternative and a meaningful contrast for the customer. It does not prove competition is absent, set pricing, or describe the full business model.
questionBank.skill: Analyze whether a contrast is meaningful differentiation.

questionBank.prompt: A campus lending service claims it will “keep coursework moving during unexpected laptop repairs.” Which conclusion is justified before supporting evidence is gathered?
options: The service is guaranteed to be adopted by students.
The claim contains an assumption that quick access to a replacement device matters in that situation.
The service has already proven its product-market fit.
The team can skip considering other ways students obtain devices.
questionBank.explanation: B correctly identifies an assumption inside the value proposition. The other choices turn the claim into proof of adoption or fit, or ignore relevant alternatives without evidence.
questionBank.skill: Recognize assumptions embedded in an expected-benefit claim.

title: Market Research
in30Seconds: Market research is the purposeful collection and interpretation of information about a market so a team can make a particular decision with less guesswork. It can use primary research, which creates new data for a specific question, and secondary research, which uses existing data. The useful question is not “Can we find data?” but “What evidence would change this decision, and what can this evidence honestly support?”
whyItMatters: Entrepreneurs routinely encounter numbers, survey results, reports, customer comments, and confident claims about demand. Market-research literacy helps them sort those inputs by question, source, population, method, and uncertainty. It supports better planning because a local demographic estimate, a small convenience survey, and a firsthand observation are not interchangeable kinds of evidence. It also protects people: responsible research treats participation as voluntary and handles personal information carefully. Good research reduces avoidable uncertainty; it does not certify a product, forecast revenue, or guarantee that a venture will succeed.
learningObjectives: Define market research as decision-focused collection and interpretation of market evidence.
Distinguish primary research from secondary research and match each to an appropriate question.
Define population, sampling frame, and sample, and explain how each limits a claim.
Interpret a research finding with its uncertainty, method, and relevant scope rather than as proof.
Apply basic ethical principles for voluntary participation and responsible handling of personal information.

collegeVersion.heading: Start with a decision and a question
collegeVersion.body:
Market research is not a pile of charts or a ritual performed before launching a project. It is the purposeful collection and interpretation of information about a market in order to inform a decision. OpenStax describes it as collecting and analyzing information related to a target market, while the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) frames it as bringing together consumer behavior and economic trends to improve an idea. In practice, a research effort earns its place when it links a question, evidence, and a decision that could change.

For example, a neighborhood grocery-delivery team may need to decide whether to investigate late-evening pickup. Its questions could be: Which nearby areas contain potential users? Are households concentrated near the proposed pickup point? What times do people report as inconvenient? How common is that constraint among the defined group? What alternatives already exist? These are different questions. A local population count can describe context, but it cannot establish why people make a particular choice. A small set of direct responses can reveal possible reasons or routines, but it cannot automatically estimate prevalence in a neighborhood.

Write the decision before choosing a method. “Learn about our customers” is too broad to guide evidence. “Decide whether to spend another week studying evening pickup for commuters within two miles of campus” is narrower. It identifies a group, geography, decision horizon, and uncertainty. A research question should also make clear what result would matter. If the team will continue studying the idea when evidence suggests a sizeable, reachable group with an unmet timing constraint, it should say what counts as suggestive evidence and what remains unknown. This is not a formula for approving or rejecting a business. It is a discipline for avoiding data collection that cannot affect the next move.

Market research touches related topics without replacing them. Customer discovery concentrates on testing a focused segment-and-problem assumption. Customer interviews are one way to gather direct evidence, but their recruiting and conversation mechanics are a separate lesson. Competitor analysis examines particular alternatives and firms. Value-proposition work frames a proposed customer benefit. This lesson stays at the research-design level: define the question, choose evidence fit for that question, and report the boundary of what was learned.

collegeVersion.heading: Primary and secondary research answer different questions
collegeVersion.body:
Primary research creates new data to answer a defined question. It might include a survey, structured observation, experiment, or group discussion, depending on the question and ethical constraints. The decisive feature is not the tool but the purpose: the team is gathering information it did not previously have. Primary research can be especially useful when the question is specific to a local setting, a new behavior, or a proposed attribute that no existing dataset measures. It requires time, design choices, and careful interpretation.

Secondary research uses data, reports, records, or other information that another organization collected earlier. It often answers broad and quantifiable questions about population, demographics, incomes, employment, industries, locations, or trends. The SBA cautions that existing sources may not be specific to one audience even when they are useful context. A researcher should therefore inspect who collected the information, when, where, for what original purpose, how key terms were defined, and whether the population matches the current question. A national figure may be sound for the nation and still be weak evidence for one campus, neighborhood, or narrow customer group.

Official sources can be a sensible starting point for secondary research. Census Business Builder, for example, provides selected demographic and economic data by location and business type. NAICS is the federal classification system used for U.S. business-economy statistics, so it can help a researcher locate data whose industry category is stated rather than guessed. Neither tool creates evidence of a specific venture’s demand. They provide context that must be connected cautiously to the claim at hand.

Primary and secondary evidence are often complementary. Suppose a team is considering a pickup point near campus. Secondary data may help describe nearby households, income measures, and relevant business categories. A direct study may then investigate a narrow practical question, such as the timing or access constraints of a defined group. The first does not replace the second, and the second does not erase the first. Combining sources is useful only when each source is allowed to answer the question it can actually support.

collegeVersion.heading: Population, sampling frame, and sample set the boundary of a claim
collegeVersion.body:
A population is the full group a research claim is about: for example, all enrolled commuter students who attend evening classes at one campus during a stated term. A sampling frame is the practical list or route from which a sample can be reached: perhaps a mailing list, a course roster, a customer database, or people who see a posted link. A sample is the portion that actually provides data. These three groups are frequently mistaken for one another. A campus newsletter list is not automatically all commuter students; the people who choose to answer a link are not automatically representative of everyone on that list.

The sampling frame matters because it reveals who could have been included and who was missed. A survey posted only in one social-media group may miss people who do not use that group. A response-based sample can also differ from nonrespondents in ways that matter to the question. Wording, timing, incentives, and the measurement itself can introduce additional limits. A large number of responses does not repair a mismatch between the intended population and the people reached.

Sample size still matters, but in a narrower way. For estimates based on samples, the Census Bureau explains that larger samples generally have less sampling error, and margins of error communicate uncertainty associated with sampling. That does not turn a margin of error into a universal accuracy label. It does not include every possible source of error, such as incomplete coverage, nonresponse, unclear questions, incorrect recording, or a conclusion that exceeds the data. The AAPOR ethics code similarly says that claims of precision and applicability to a broader population must be warranted by the sampling frame and methods used.

Report the scope before stating a finding. “Among 26 voluntary respondents reached through a campus newsletter, 14 reported a late-evening pickup problem” is a bounded description. “More than half of all commuters need this service” is a population claim that the same convenience sample cannot establish. The first can justify a next research question; the second requires a design that can support generalization.

collegeVersion.heading: Interpret evidence honestly and handle people responsibly
collegeVersion.body:
Interpretation begins by separating what the evidence observed from what the team infers. An estimate should travel with its population, date, source, method, and relevant uncertainty. A pattern may be a promising signal, a challenge to an assumption, or a reason to investigate a subgroup. It is not automatically proof of demand, willingness to pay, a market-size estimate, or a forecast. When sources conflict, do not average them into confidence. Check whether they used different geographies, time periods, definitions, samples, or measures. The disagreement may identify the next useful question.

Research involving people also has ethical obligations. Participation should be voluntary, and people should not be misled about the purpose of the activity. If identifiable information is collected, researchers should be truthful about its use, restrict access, and follow applicable rules. The Federal Trade Commission’s business guidance emphasizes data minimization: do not collect or retain sensitive personal information without a legitimate need, keep what is needed only as long as necessary, protect it, and dispose of it properly. Exact legal duties vary by jurisdiction, organization, and data type, so this lesson is a general ethical baseline rather than legal advice.

A compact research record helps make conclusions reviewable: state the decision; write the research question; identify the population and the accessible sampling frame; name the sources and dates; describe how the information was obtained; distinguish observations from interpretations; and list limitations and remaining uncertainty. This record makes it possible for a later reader to challenge an inference without losing the underlying evidence. Market research is most useful when it makes both the next decision and the limits of confidence clearer.

vocabulary.definition: Purposeful collection and interpretation of information about a market to inform a defined decision.
A specific question that identifies what information is needed and what decision the answer could inform.
Research that collects new data to answer a particular question or set of questions.
Research that analyzes existing data or reports collected previously by another entity or for another purpose.
The full group that a research claim intends to describe, defined by relevant characteristics, place, and time.
The practical list, database, channel, or procedure through which members of a population can be reached for a study.
The subset of people, organizations, or records from which a study actually obtains information.
Uncertainty that arises because an estimate is calculated from a sample rather than every member of the population.
A stated range that communicates sampling uncertainty around an estimate at a specified confidence level; it does not cover every source of error.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Market research is like checking the facts before choosing where to build a playground. You might look at a map to see where families live, read a report about the neighborhood, and ask a carefully chosen group what times they use the park. Each clue answers a different question. A map cannot tell you what children enjoy, and a few conversations cannot tell you what every family thinks.

The important habit is to label each clue honestly: where it came from, whom it describes, and what it cannot prove. If people share information with you, be fair—let them choose whether to take part, explain how you will use their information, and do not collect private details you do not need.
eli10.analogy: Think of market research as packing for a trip by checking several kinds of information. A weather forecast helps with temperature, a road map helps with the route, and a message from a friend helps with one local detail. You would not use the road map to predict rain or treat one friend’s experience as a complete guide to every road. Good research matches each source to the question it can answer.
eli10.analogyLimits: A trip plan is usually about one traveler, while market research often makes claims about groups of people and must account for sampling, privacy, and uncertainty. Evidence can guide a decision, but unlike a packing list it cannot make a business outcome certain.

workedExample: A campus team is considering whether to study a late-evening grocery pickup service. Its decision is not whether to launch; it is whether the idea deserves more research. First, it uses Census Business Builder and local transit schedules to describe the surrounding area and possible access constraints. Those sources provide context, not proof that people would use a pickup point. Next, the team posts a voluntary questionnaire through one campus newsletter. Twenty-six people respond, and 14 say that grocery access after 8 p.m. is difficult. The team records the sampling frame (newsletter recipients) and the sample (the 26 respondents), so it does not claim that 54% of all students or local residents have the problem. It reports a directional pattern among respondents, notes the likely coverage and self-selection limits, stores no unnecessary identifiers, and considers a next study with a population and sampling plan suited to estimating how common the constraint is. The evidence supports continued inquiry, not a demand forecast or a launch decision.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting with a favorite method or dataset instead of a decision-relevant question.
commonMistakes.correction: State the decision, population, and uncertainty first; then choose evidence that can change the next move.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating secondary data as automatically specific to the current audience.
commonMistakes.correction: Check the source’s geography, time period, definitions, collection purpose, and population before applying it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a large or convenient sample as representative by default.
commonMistakes.correction: Report the population, sampling frame, selection process, response limits, and sampling uncertainty; size alone cannot establish generalizability.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting an interesting pattern as proof of demand or a forecast.
commonMistakes.correction: State what was observed, scope the inference to the evidence, and identify the next uncertainty.

commonMistakes.mistake: Collecting identifiable or sensitive information simply because it might be useful later.
commonMistakes.correction: Collect only what is needed for the stated purpose, explain use honestly, restrict access, protect it, and dispose of it when no longer needed.

compareContrast.distinction: Primary research creates new information for a current question; secondary research analyzes information already collected, often for a different purpose.
The population is the full group a claim concerns; the sample is the subset from which information was actually obtained.
Sampling error concerns uncertainty from observing a sample; it does not include every problem caused by coverage, response, measurement, or interpretation.

keyTakeaway: Market research earns trust by matching evidence to a specific decision and by stating what the evidence cannot establish. Use primary and secondary sources for the questions they fit, define the population and sample clearly, protect participants and data, and treat uncertainty as information rather than something to hide.

questionBank.prompt: Which research question is most likely to guide a useful market-research decision?
options: Among defined evening commuters within two miles of campus, what access constraint should we investigate before deciding whether to study pickup service further?
Can we collect as many facts as possible about customers?
Will our business definitely succeed if people like the idea?
Which answer makes our proposed service sound most exciting?
questionBank.explanation: A is specific about a population, a decision, and an uncertainty. B is too broad to select evidence, C asks for a guarantee research cannot provide, and D treats research as promotion rather than inquiry.
questionBank.skill: Identify a decision-focused research question.

questionBank.prompt: A team needs current, location-specific context on population and economic characteristics before deciding where to investigate a service. Which is the best starting source type?
options: A list of positive comments from the team’s friends
Official secondary data with a stated geography, date, and definitions, such as relevant Census data
A claim that a similar service succeeded somewhere else
A forecast that assumes every nearby resident will become a customer
questionBank.explanation: B is appropriate secondary context because it identifies the data source, geography, date, and definitions. Friend comments are not a population estimate, a distant success does not establish local conditions, and the forecast assumes adoption without evidence.
questionBank.skill: Match a broad contextual question to appropriate secondary research.

questionBank.prompt: A questionnaire link in one campus newsletter receives 80 responses. Which conclusion is most justified?
options: The responses automatically represent every student because 80 is a large number.
The margin of error, if calculated, would eliminate any concern about who saw or answered the link.
The responses describe the people who answered, but claims about all students require a population and sampling approach that supports that generalization.
The team should discard the responses because nonrepresentative evidence can never guide a next question.
questionBank.explanation: C states the evidence boundary. A mistakes size for representativeness, B confuses sampling uncertainty with coverage and response problems, and D wrongly treats directional evidence as useless.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish a sample description from a population claim.

questionBank.prompt: Which practice best reflects ethical handling of personal information collected for market research?
options: Collect every identifier that might be useful in a future project, even if it is unrelated to the current question.
Promise anonymity but keep names attached to responses for convenience.
Share raw identifiable responses with anyone on the project so more people can analyze them.
Explain the purpose and use of identifiable data, collect only what is needed, limit access, protect it, and dispose of it when it is no longer needed.
questionBank.explanation: D follows voluntary, transparent, and minimized data handling. A increases unnecessary risk, B is misleading, and C exposes data beyond a need-to-know basis.
questionBank.skill: Apply ethical data-minimization and access principles.

questionBank.prompt: What does a reported margin of error most directly communicate about a sample-based estimate?
options: The uncertainty associated with using a sample rather than the whole population, at a stated confidence level
That the study has no coverage, response, wording, or recording errors
That any result inside the range proves market demand
That the sample must represent every group equally
questionBank.explanation: A is the bounded role of a margin of error. B claims it covers all sources of error, C turns uncertainty information into proof, and D asserts representativeness without examining the sampling frame or method.
questionBank.skill: Interpret sampling uncertainty without overstating it.

title: Competitor Analysis
in30Seconds: Competitor analysis is a structured comparison of the alternatives a potential customer can choose. It includes direct competitors offering a similar solution, indirect competitors solving the same task differently, and non-consumption choices such as a workaround or doing nothing. Compare only dimensions that matter to the customer and the decision at hand. Record what is observed separately from what you infer, then use the result to frame questions—not to predict victory.
whyItMatters: A narrow list of firms can make an idea look more original than it is. Competitor analysis asks what people actually use, avoid, or tolerate when they face a task. It can reveal a neglected segment, inconvenient channel, missing service, or constraint worth investigating. In coursework and practice, its value is disciplined comparison: it supports a reasoned next step while avoiding the unsupported claim that a rival is weak or that a new venture will succeed.
learningObjectives: Define competitor analysis and distinguish direct, indirect, and non-consumption alternatives.
Identify comparison dimensions that are relevant to a specified customer task.
Separate observable competitor facts from inferences about customers or future outcomes.
Apply an ethical, public-information approach to a small competitive analysis grid.
Explain why an apparent gap is a hypothesis rather than proof of demand.

collegeVersion.heading: Start with alternatives, not a flattering list of rivals
collegeVersion.body:
Competitor analysis is a purposeful comparison of alternatives available to people in a defined situation. The U.S. Small Business Administration describes it as a way to learn from businesses competing for potential customers and to identify a possible competitive edge. That purpose matters: the analysis does not ask merely, “Which companies look like ours?” It asks, “What could a particular person choose when trying to accomplish this task?”

Direct competitors provide a closely similar product or service to a similar customer segment. A neighborhood bicycle-repair shop and another local bicycle-repair shop are direct alternatives for a commuter with a broken chain. Indirect competitors address the same underlying task through a different offering: a sporting-goods store that sells repair kits, a mobile mechanic, or a bike-share membership may reduce the need for that shop in some situations. A third category is non-consumption: postponing the repair, borrowing a bicycle, walking, repairing it oneself, or simply accepting the inconvenience. Non-consumption is not a formal claim that every person is a customer. It is a reminder to include realistic workarounds and the option not to buy.

The set changes with the segment and use case. A competitive set for a student needing a same-day repair may differ from one for a recreational rider planning a weekend trip. Geography, access, timing, budget, quality expectations, and switching costs all change which alternatives are plausible. Therefore write the comparison boundary explicitly: for example, “same-day bicycle-mobility options for campus commuters within three miles.” A broad label such as “the transportation market” makes a grid vague; a boundary that is too narrow can hide meaningful substitutes. The aim is a defensible working set, which can be revised as better evidence emerges.

collegeVersion.heading: Compare customer-relevant dimensions consistently
collegeVersion.body:
After naming alternatives, choose a small set of dimensions that matters to the customer task. The SBA suggests examining competition by product or service line and market segment, and it names such landscape features as strengths and weaknesses, entry barriers, market share, target-market importance, and indirect competitors. OpenStax similarly presents a competitive analysis grid that identifies competitors and assesses strengths, weaknesses, and key success factors. Those are prompts, not a mandatory universal template. A campus meal-delivery service might compare delivery window, dietary coverage, pickup location, price range, ordering friction, and reliability. A B2B scheduling tool might compare integration, setup effort, administrative control, accessibility, and support.

A useful grid keeps the same definition for each column. “Fast” is not a usable dimension unless the comparison states what is measured, such as advertised delivery window or observed time from order to pickup. “High quality” should be replaced by observable features, documented standards, or carefully attributed customer feedback. Price can be a listed price, a price range, or total cost under stated assumptions; it should not be an impression disguised as a fact. The same care applies to geographic coverage, hours, return terms, features, availability, and public claims.

Do not turn the grid into a scorecard designed to crown the founder's idea. It is more useful when it surfaces trade-offs. A competitor may offer a lower price because it limits service hours; another may offer extensive support but require a longer setup. Whether either trade-off is favorable depends on a customer and context, not on a generic ranking. Market share can be relevant where reliable, comparable data exist, but it is often unavailable or poorly matched to a narrow segment. It should never be guessed from search-result order, social-media follower counts, or a founder's intuition. The analysis has done useful work if it describes an alternative landscape accurately enough to focus the next question.

collegeVersion.heading: Use evidence ethically and label inferences honestly
collegeVersion.body:
Many inputs to a first-pass competitor analysis are public: a firm's website, published prices and policies, product documentation, business directories, public filings when relevant, and lawful observation of an ordinary customer experience. Respect terms of access, do not bypass controls, do not misrepresent your identity to obtain restricted information, and do not seek or use confidential information. Do not copy another firm's protected branding, proprietary content, or internal materials. Ethical research protects people and also improves judgment: secretly obtained fragments are easy to misunderstand and hard to defend.

Keep two columns in your notes. The first holds observations with a source and date: “Company A lists weekday pickup from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on its public site, viewed August 19, 2026.” The second holds interpretations: “This may leave an evening-access gap for some commuters.” The observation can be checked. The interpretation may be sensible, but it remains a hypothesis. The distinction is crucial when a grid includes terms such as strength, weakness, customer loyalty, or intention. A stated feature is a fact about a public claim; it is not proof that customers value the feature or that the business performs as claimed.

An apparent gap also needs modest language. If no competitor advertises late-night pickup, several explanations are possible: there may be low demand, a licensing or staffing constraint, a service that is hard to find, or an opportunity. Competitive analysis can identify the question; it cannot settle it alone. The SBA distinguishes competitive analysis from broader market research, which examines customers and market conditions. That boundary helps avoid overreach. Follow-up work may test the importance of the gap, but this lesson does not prescribe a research design or interview method.

The best output is a brief, dated comparison and a small list of uncertainty-aware hypotheses. It might say, “Evening access appears less visible among the reviewed alternatives; determine whether the relevant segment values it and whether safe operation is feasible.” That is neither a promise nor an attack on competitors. It is a decision-useful inference tied to evidence, open to revision, and ethically gathered.

vocabulary.definition: A structured comparison of alternatives that may compete for a defined customer's attention, spending, or use.
An alternative offering a closely similar solution to a similar customer segment.
An alternative that addresses the same underlying task through a different product, service, or method.
A choice to do without a purchase, postpone it, or rely on a workaround instead.
A table that compares a defined set of alternatives using the same relevant dimensions.
A consistently defined feature used to compare alternatives, such as access window, setup effort, or listed price.
Information that can be checked against a specified source, date, or direct observation.
A reasoned interpretation drawn from evidence that remains open to revision.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine you want a snack after practice. Your choices are not only the snack shop across the street. You could use a vending machine, eat something from your bag, go home, or decide you are not hungry enough to bother. Competitor analysis is making an honest list of those choices and comparing the things that matter, like time, cost, taste, and whether the shop is open. It is not a contest where you secretly give your own idea the best points.

Write down what you can actually check. If the shop's sign says it closes at 6 p.m., that is an observation. “Students need a later shop” is a guess that might be worth checking, but it is not proven by the sign. Keeping facts and guesses apart helps you learn without fooling yourself.
eli10.analogy: It is like comparing routes home on a map: driving, walking, taking a bus, asking for a ride, or staying where you are are all alternatives. You compare the same features for each route, such as time, cost, and reliability.
eli10.analogyLimits: People do not choose products as predictably as routes. They may have habits, preferences, access needs, or constraints that a simple grid cannot show. A comparison helps form questions; it does not forecast what everyone will do.

workedExample: Hypothetical example: A student considers a secure, staffed evening bicycle-pickup service near a campus. She lists three direct or close alternatives: two repair shops and a sporting-goods retailer with repair kits. She also lists indirect and non-consumption alternatives: a peer who can help, a bike-share pass, walking, and postponing the repair. Her grid uses published hours, listed repair services, pickup process, location, and advertised price range. She notes, as facts, that both repair shops list weekday closing times before 7 p.m. Her inference is that evening pickup may be inconvenient for some commuters. She does not call that an opportunity yet: the shops may have reasons for those hours, and commuters may not value later access enough to use or pay for it. Her next output is a hypothesis and a constraint list, not a claim that the service will win.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing only businesses with the same product name.
commonMistakes.correction: Include direct alternatives, indirect ways to complete the task, and realistic non-purchase or workaround choices.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing each competitor with different or vague criteria.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the same defined, customer-relevant dimensions for every alternative and record their sources.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a public feature or review count as proof of customer preference.
commonMistakes.correction: Label the feature as an observation and the conclusion about customer value as an inference.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling an unadvertised feature a market gap that guarantees demand.
commonMistakes.correction: Frame it as a hypothesis; low visibility can have several explanations besides opportunity.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to obtain restricted competitor information or copying protected material.
commonMistakes.correction: Use lawful public information, respect access limits, and write an original analysis.

compareContrast.distinction: A direct competitor offers a closely similar solution; an indirect competitor solves the same task through a different method.
A fact can be checked against a source or observation; an inference interprets what that evidence might mean.
Competitive analysis focuses on alternatives and their characteristics; broader market research also investigates customers and market conditions.

keyTakeaway: Competitor analysis maps the real alternatives for a defined customer task and compares them on consistent, relevant dimensions. Its strongest conclusion is a well-supported question or hypothesis, not a prediction that a new venture will succeed.

questionBank.prompt: Which option is an indirect competitor for a neighborhood bicycle-repair shop serving commuters with broken bikes?
options: A sporting-goods store that sells repair kits
Another local bicycle-repair shop
The shop's own repair counter
A supplier that ships parts only to repair shops
questionBank.explanation: A is correct because repair kits can help a commuter address the same task through a different method. B is a direct competitor, C is part of the focal business, and D is an upstream supplier rather than a customer alternative.
questionBank.skill: distinguishing indirect from direct competitors

questionBank.prompt: A student wants to compare three meal-delivery alternatives for busy evening students. Which grid design is strongest?
options: Give each alternative a different set of favorable features
Compare each alternative's published delivery window, dietary coverage, price range, and ordering steps
Rank the alternatives by the student's personal favorite
Record only the number of social-media followers
questionBank.explanation: B is correct because it uses the same task-relevant, definable dimensions for each alternative. A prevents comparison, C is an unsupported preference, and D is not a reliable proxy for fit or performance.
questionBank.skill: selecting consistent comparison dimensions

questionBank.prompt: Which note is best labeled as an inference rather than an observable fact?
options: The firm's website lists weekday hours of 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
The public menu shows no gluten-free option.
Commuters may value an evening pickup option.
The business directory places the firm two miles from campus.
questionBank.explanation: C is correct because it interprets what evidence might mean for a segment. A, B, and D can be checked against named public sources at a stated time, although they still need verification.
questionBank.skill: separating facts from inferences

questionBank.prompt: A founder finds no nearby competitor advertising late-night service. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Late-night service will certainly be profitable.
Nearby firms have intentionally ignored their customers.
The founder has no competitors because the feature is absent.
Late-night access is a hypothesis worth investigating, since low visibility can have several explanations.
questionBank.explanation: D is correct because an apparent gap can suggest a question without proving demand, feasibility, or competitor intent. A, B, and C make claims that the observation cannot establish.
questionBank.skill: interpreting an apparent market gap cautiously

questionBank.prompt: Which action best follows an ethical approach to competitor analysis?
options: Create a false identity to request a rival's restricted internal pricing file
Copy a rival's branded comparison chart into a pitch deck
Record public prices and policies with dates, then write original notes about possible trade-offs
Publish a competitor employee's private contact information to recruit customers
questionBank.explanation: C is correct because it relies on public information, documents the observation, and uses original analysis. A seeks restricted information deceptively, B may misuse protected material, and D violates privacy.
questionBank.skill: applying ethical research boundaries

title: Business Models
in30Seconds: A business model is the linked logic of how an organization creates value, gets that value to people, and captures enough resources to continue operating. It connects an offering and its users with the work, partners, channels, revenues, and costs that make the offering possible. A business model is not a guarantee of demand, profit, or growth. It is a set of testable assumptions whose parts must fit together.
whyItMatters: A good idea can fail as a venture if its delivery work is impractical or its resources do not cover the cost of continuing. Learning to describe a business model helps students see these connected choices before treating a product, a revenue label, or a marketing claim as the whole venture. It also makes comparisons more precise: two organizations can offer similar benefits while using very different ways to deliver them and sustain their work. That reasoning supports later work on the Business Model Canvas, pricing, startup costs, and financial projections without replacing any of them.
learningObjectives: Define a business model as the connected logic of value creation, delivery, and capture.
Distinguish a business model from a business plan, a value proposition, and a revenue model.
Explain common revenue arrangements and the trade-offs they introduce.
Analyze how fixed and variable costs affect the fit of a proposed business model.
Apply a consistency check to identify an unsupported link in a hypothetical business model.

collegeVersion.heading: A business model is a connected explanation, not a label
collegeVersion.body:
A business model explains how an organization intends to create value, deliver that value, and capture resources from the activity. OpenStax describes it as the rationale for how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value, while noting that the term has more than one accepted definition. The useful common idea is connection. An offering, a customer group, a way of reaching people, the work required, and the financial consequences are not separate answers on a worksheet; together they describe how the organization is supposed to function.

Value creation concerns the benefit the organization aims to make possible for customers, users, or other stakeholders. Value delivery concerns the activities, resources, partners, and access paths that make the benefit available. Value capture concerns how the organization receives money or other resources and what it gives up to operate. In a for-profit setting, revenue and costs are central to value capture. In a mission-driven organization, grants, donations, or contracts may also be part of the resource logic, alongside the intended beneficiary value. None of those sources of support proves that the model works; each is an assumption that must be examined.

Several nearby terms should stay distinct. A value proposition is a bounded claim about an expected benefit for a customer in a context. It is one input to a business model, not the whole model. A revenue model describes the particular way money enters the organization, such as a one-time sale or recurring subscription. A business plan is a broader planning document that may set out operations, evidence, goals, risks, and implementation. Strategy concerns choices about how an organization will compete or pursue its mission. These tools can inform one another, but substituting one for another can hide a missing connection. This lesson does not teach the nine Business Model Canvas blocks, set prices, or prepare financial projections; those are separate methods for examining parts of the larger logic.

collegeVersion.heading: Revenue arrangements describe who pays, when, and for what
collegeVersion.body:
A revenue arrangement answers a narrow but essential question: from whom will the organization receive money, in exchange for what, and on what occasion? A transactional arrangement collects money when a customer buys a product or service. Its advantage is clarity: payment is tied to a defined purchase. Its trade-off is that revenue depends on repeat purchases or a steady flow of new purchases. A subscription arrangement exchanges recurring payment for continuing access or continuing service. It can make the timing of revenue more regular, but it also creates an ongoing obligation to provide value that customers judge worth renewing.

A usage-based arrangement charges in relation to a measurable use, such as a delivery, a completed transaction, or computing capacity. It can align payment with consumption, yet it requires a clear and trusted way to measure use; revenue can vary as customers use more or less. In a commission or marketplace arrangement, an intermediary may receive a fee when it helps other parties complete a transaction. This can let the intermediary serve a market without owning every item exchanged, but it depends on attracting and maintaining trust among more than one group. OpenStax’s digital-business-model discussion also describes advertising-supported and freemium arrangements. Advertising-supported content may be free to the audience because advertisers pay for access or attention; the organization must therefore serve both its audience and its advertisers. Freemium offers a basic version without payment and seeks paid upgrades for added access or features; free users still create service and support demands.

These categories are descriptive, not rankings. A subscription is not automatically better than a sale, and an advertising arrangement is not automatically sustainable simply because users do not pay directly. An organization may combine arrangements, but each combination raises questions. Who receives the main benefit? Who pays? What behavior triggers payment? What evidence suggests that the payer will accept that exchange? The pricing lesson addresses how an organization might set an amount. Here, the task is only to identify the revenue relationship and its operational implications.

collegeVersion.heading: Cost structure and delivery choices test whether the links fit
collegeVersion.body:
Cost structure is the pattern of resources an organization must use or pay for to deliver its offering. A fixed cost does not change directly with each additional unit over a relevant short period; examples can include a lease, a basic software subscription, or salaries committed for that period. A variable cost changes with activity, such as materials used in each order, packaging, shipping, or a per-transaction payment fee. The distinction is contextual. A cost that is fixed for a month may be changed later by renegotiating a contract or adding capacity. It is a tool for reasoning about the relationship between activity and resources, not a permanent label.

Delivery choices reshape this pattern. A venture that produces and stores its own goods may take on equipment, inventory, quality-control, and storage commitments. A venture that uses a partner for fulfillment may avoid some direct commitments but become dependent on that partner’s reliability, terms, and capacity. Neither arrangement is universally preferable. The question is whether the delivery choice can support the promised benefit while the revenue arrangement can plausibly support the resulting obligations. A low-friction digital download, a time-intensive local service, and a marketplace that verifies transactions each need different resources and expose different points of failure.

A simple consistency check can reveal a weak model. State the value claim, the people who receive it, the path by which they receive it, the payer and payment trigger, and the main delivery obligations. Then ask what must be true for every link to hold. If a service promises immediate help but relies on a single partner with no available capacity at busy times, delivery is uncertain. If an app is free to users and relies on advertisers, the model must explain why there will be enough audience attention and advertiser demand to support the service. These are hypotheses to test with evidence, not forecasts to announce. A business model can be revised when a link fails; revision is not proof that the original story was irrational, but it should be guided by what the organization learns.

vocabulary.definition: The connected logic by which an organization creates value, delivers it, and captures resources needed to operate.
Producing or enabling a benefit that a customer, user, or stakeholder may find worthwhile.
The activities, resources, partners, and access paths used to make an offering available to its intended users.
The way an organization receives money or other resources and bears the costs of providing its offering.
The specific arrangement through which money enters an organization, including who pays, for what, and when.
A cost that does not change directly with each additional unit of activity over a stated relevant period.
A cost that changes with the level of activity, output, or transactions.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Think of a school snack stand. Its idea is not just “sell snacks.” It needs a connected story: which snacks help hungry students, how the stand gets them, where students can buy them, who pays, and whether the money coming in can cover buying the snacks and running the stand. That connected story is its business model.

Different stories can work differently. One stand might sell each snack one time. Another might offer a weekly snack pass. A website might let visitors use it free because advertisers pay instead. None of these labels tells us automatically that the idea will work. We still need to ask whether people want the benefit, whether the stand can deliver it reliably, and whether the resources coming in can support the work.
eli10.analogy: A business model is like planning a school play. The show needs a reason people want to attend, a way to rehearse and perform it, tickets or another source of support, and enough materials and help to put it on. If one part changes—such as the venue becoming unavailable—the rest of the plan may need to change too.
eli10.analogyLimits: A play usually has one event and a clear ticket moment, while organizations can serve several groups continuously and use complicated contracts, regulations, and cost patterns. The analogy also does not decide whether a venture is ethical, legal, or financially viable; those questions require separate evidence.

workedExample: HarborLoop is a hypothetical service that lets neighborhood residents reserve time with shared cargo bicycles. Its value claim is convenient short trips for people who occasionally need to carry more than they can hold. To deliver that value, it needs bicycles in working condition, reservation software, safe storage locations, maintenance, and a way for riders to access the bikes. Its proposed revenue arrangement is a fee for each completed reservation, so payment is linked to use rather than a membership. The model therefore has variable costs such as payment processing and repairs associated with use, plus costs that may stay relatively fixed for a period, such as storage agreements and basic software. A consistency check reveals an assumption: if bikes are often unavailable at the times residents need them, the service cannot deliver its convenience claim even if its payment system works. HarborLoop might test availability and maintenance patterns, then revise its locations, staffing, or access arrangement. This example identifies a model; it does not set a fee, forecast revenue, or recommend that anyone start the service.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a revenue label the entire business model.
commonMistakes.correction: A subscription, sale, or advertising label states only one part of the linked value, delivery, and resource logic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming users and payers must be the same people.
commonMistakes.correction: They may be the same, but advertising-supported and marketplace arrangements show why each group’s role should be stated separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating fixed costs as costs that can never change.
commonMistakes.correction: Fixed means not directly tied to each unit over a relevant period; contracts and capacity can change later.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a promising offering proves financial viability.
commonMistakes.correction: An offering can be valuable while its delivery commitments or resource arrangement remain impractical.

compareContrast.distinction: A business model links value, delivery, and resource logic; a revenue model specifies only how money enters the organization.
A fixed cost does not change directly with each unit in a stated period; a variable cost changes with activity or output.
A value proposition states an expected customer benefit; a business model explains the broader system intended to provide and sustain it.

keyTakeaway: A business model is a connected, revisable explanation of how value is created, delivered, and supported by revenue and other resources. A sound analysis checks whether each link can plausibly support the others instead of treating a product idea or revenue label as a complete answer.

A document that guarantees a venture will earn a profit.

A visual worksheet with a required number of boxes.

questionBank.prompt: A music-learning service charges members every month for continuing access to lessons. Which trade-off follows most directly from this subscription arrangement?
options: It removes the need to keep providing value after the first payment.
It creates an ongoing obligation to provide access or service that members judge worth renewing.
It guarantees that every member will use the lessons equally often.
It means the service has no fixed costs.
questionBank.explanation: A subscription exchanges recurring payment for continuing value, so renewal depends on the ongoing offering. It does not eliminate service obligations, guarantee usage, or determine the cost structure.
questionBank.skill: Explain an operational implication of recurring revenue.

questionBank.prompt: A platform lets readers use its articles without payment and receives money from advertisers. Which analysis best identifies the business-model issue?
options: The platform has no customers because readers do not pay.
The platform needs only attractive articles; delivery and costs are irrelevant.
The platform must consider how it serves readers while also attracting advertisers whose payments support the service.
The platform has automatically proven that advertising will cover its costs.
questionBank.explanation: Advertising-supported arrangements can involve different users and payers. The organization must create and deliver value for readers and a reason for advertisers to pay; neither fact guarantees enough revenue.
questionBank.skill: Analyze the roles of users and payers in an advertising-supported arrangement.

questionBank.prompt: Which scenario is the clearest warning that a proposed business model may have a delivery mismatch?
options: A service uses a name that its founders like.
A team writes its idea on a slide before discussing it.
A venture has both a fixed cost and a variable cost.
A same-day repair promise depends on a single technician who is unavailable during the busiest hours.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement about fixed and variable costs is most accurate?

Every organization has the same mix of fixed and variable costs.

questionBank.skill: Distinguish fixed and variable costs with the relevant time boundary.
